Early College High Schools in AIR's admissions-lottery study
Early College High Schools in the AIR study: ten admissions-lottery sites in five states, with cost estimates available for six sites.
https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED602451.pdf
AIR evaluated 2,458 applicants to 10 Early College High Schools using admissions lotteries in five states.

The 2005–06 through 2007–08 applicant cohorts included 1,044 students offered enrollment and 1,414 not offered. The outcome estimates are intent-to-treat effects of an offer, not separate evidence from the report’s complier analysis.
Lottery-based intent-to-treat evaluation of an offer of enrollment in 10 Early College High Schools versus no offer; Year 10 is six years after expected high-school graduation.
Song et al. (2019), pp. 3–4; Appendix F.
An Early College offer increased any college enrollment by Year 10 by 7.2 percentage points (84.2% versus 77.0%; p < .001).

This is the intent-to-treat effect of being offered enrollment in the 10-school lottery study. It measures any postsecondary enrollment by Year 10, not degree completion or an effect for every Early College model.
Percentage-point intent-to-treat difference in any college enrollment by Year 10, offer minus no offer.
Exhibit F-1, PDF p. 76.
An Early College offer increased any postsecondary degree by Year 10 by 11.9 percentage points (45.4% versus 33.5%; p < .001).
This intent-to-treat estimate covers any postsecondary degree in the lottery-study sample. It does not isolate a particular Early College component or establish a lifetime earnings effect.
Percentage-point intent-to-treat difference in earning any postsecondary degree by Year 10, offer minus no offer.
Exhibit F-3, PDF p. 79.
An Early College offer increased associate-degree or certificate attainment by Year 10 by 18.2 percentage points (29.3% versus 11.1%; p < .001).
This is the intent-to-treat effect for associate degrees or certificates in the lottery-study sample. It should not be combined with the bachelor’s estimate as independent study evidence.
Percentage-point intent-to-treat difference in associate-degree or certificate attainment by Year 10, offer minus no offer.
Exhibit F-3, PDF p. 79.
An Early College offer increased bachelor’s-degree attainment by Year 10 by 5.2 percentage points (30.1% versus 24.9%; p = .037).
This is the intent-to-treat bachelor’s-degree result from the same lottery evaluation and horizon as the other attainment records. It is not a separate replication.
Percentage-point intent-to-treat difference in bachelor’s-degree attainment by Year 10, offer minus no offer.
Exhibit F-3, PDF p. 79.
An Early College offer showed a 0.8-point difference in four-year-college enrollment by Year 10 (57.6% versus 56.7%; p = .744).
The report’s intent-to-treat estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero for this outcome. It does not negate the study’s other enrollment and degree findings.
Percentage-point intent-to-treat difference in enrollment at a four-year college by Year 10, offer minus no offer.
Exhibit F-1, PDF p. 76.
AIR’s model estimated $57,682 in lifetime private and public benefits per Early College student (2017 dollars).

This is a source-reported modeled lifetime value from estimated attainment differences and prior-return studies, not observed earnings. The preferred estimate combines $33,709 private and $23,973 public benefits.
2017 USD modeled lifetime private and public benefits per Early College student, attributed through estimated postsecondary-attainment differences.
Atchison et al. (2019), Table 1, PDF p. 11.

AIR estimated a midpoint additional cost of $3,819 per Early College student over four high-school years (2017 dollars).

The source averages the midpoint yearly cost difference ($955) across six Early College–traditional-high-school comparisons. It includes school spending, college instruction, and incremental dual-enrollment administration, while some centralized costs such as transportation were not fully captured.
2017 USD modeled incremental cost per Early College student over four high-school years, midpoint across six Early College–traditional-school comparisons.
Atchison et al. (2019), pp. 11–15; Figure 3.

AIR’s preferred model estimated a $53,863 net present value per Early College student (2017 dollars).
The paper defines net present value as modeled lifetime benefits minus modeled incremental four-year cost. This is not a measured participant payment or a result from a separate experiment.
2017 USD source-reported modeled net present value per Early College student: total modeled benefits ($57,682) less midpoint modeled four-year incremental cost ($3,819).
Atchison et al. (2019), Figure 4 and p. 15.

AIR’s preferred model reported a 15.1 benefit-to-cost ratio for Early College High Schools.

This source-reported model divides $57,682 in estimated lifetime private and public benefits by the $3,819 midpoint incremental cost. It is not an observed return or a universal estimate across Early College sites.
Source-reported modeled benefit-to-cost ratio using average lifetime benefits and midpoint four-year incremental costs, 2017 dollars.
Atchison et al. (2019), Figure 4 and p. 15.
USD
Modeled lifetime benefits divided by modeled four-year incremental Early College cost; source scenario, not an observed return.
AIR’s conservative model reported a 4.6 benefit-to-cost ratio for Early College High Schools.
The source combines $34,834 in conservative modeled benefits with a $7,615 upper-bound four-year cost. It remains a scenario analysis rather than an observed rate of return.
Source-reported conservative modeled benefit-to-cost ratio using lower-bound benefits and upper-bound four-year incremental costs, 2017 dollars.
Atchison et al. (2019), p. 15.

Modeled lifetime benefits divided by modeled four-year incremental Early College cost; source scenario, not an observed return.
